name: fosterage

attributes.attribute: bond five times more durable than blood
fostered training in druidic arts, war, and householding

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fosterage was an Irish social custom. Families did not raise their own noble offspring themselves. Unrelated people took them in and raised them. The practice tied families and territories together. Many held the bond of fosterage as five times more durable than the bond of blood. Children gained training in druidic arts, war, and householding. Their food and lodging matched the social standing of their own family. Children raised together in a single home were called foster brothers and sisters even without a blood tie. The most intense bonds in Irish mythology run between fosterlings. The combat of the hero Cuchulainn against his foster brother Ferdiad reaches Ferdiad's death after three days. Fostering by the mother's brother counted as a common choice. His mother's brother, king Conchobar mac Nessa, brought him up in the royal court. Reliance on the maternal uncle shows the matrilineal line carried weight in Irish law alongside strict limits on women's rights. The tie of uncle to fosterling nearly matched parent to child. It also bound the fosterling to care for the foster parents in their old age. The arrangement therefore formed bonds that were legal and financial as well as emotional.

okr.objective: Fosterage was the Irish custom of raising noble children away from their kin.
key_results: Fosterage bonds ran five times as durable as the bond of blood.
Foster children learned druidic arts, war, and householding.
The hero Cuchulainn fought his foster brother Ferdiad.
Fostering by the maternal uncle carried legal weight in Irish law.
